title: control-plane-service-ownership-map
content:
Purpose: capture proposed service boundaries for the control plane, assign ownership, and call out routing policy responsibilities across multi-region deployments. This is intentionally lightweight — meant as a single-pane reference for platform engineers and infra architects.

High-level goals:
- Clear ownership for API gateway, orchestration layer, and runtime adapters.
- Minimal coupling: control plane components communicate over stable, versioned RPC/HTTP interfaces.
- Routing policies expressible as data (policies + priorities) rather than bespoke code across services.
- Multi-region behavior (primary/secondary, regional failover, data residency) documented per component.

Definitions / scope:
- API Gateway: ingress point for tenant requests (hosted API and control-plane APIs). Responsibilities: auth, rate-limiting, tenant routing, request shaping, tenant-aware telemetry tags. Not responsible for deployment orchestration or long-term state.
- Orchestration (Control Plane Core): handles lifecycle operations (deploy, scale, rollback), policy evaluation (routing, fallback), and matchmaking between logical routes and available runtime adapters. Owns desired state and rollout workflows (canaries, A/B).
- Runtime Adapters: lightweight adapters for specific runtime classes (hosted GPUs, dedicated pools, private on-prem adapter). Responsible for executing workloads, reporting health/metrics, and exposing a standardized runtime API (StartSession, ExtendKV, StreamTokens).
- Policy Store: backing store for routing and placement policies. Exposed via read APIs and watched by orchestration. Policies are versioned artifacts (policy_id + schema).
- Regional Control Agents: small proxies co-located with regional infra to provide low-latency decisions (caching policy fragments, fast path routing for low-latency SLOs). They do not own global policy: they cache and report telemetry and local health.

Proposed service boundaries and ownership:
- API Gateway (team: platform-engineering-networking)
  - Owns: auth plug-ins (OIDC/JWT integrations), per-tenant rate limits, basic tenant routing to orchestration endpoints, edge TLS, WAF rules for control-plane endpoints.
  - SLOs: 99.95% availability for control-plane ingress, P99 latency < 50ms for auth+route decision.
  - Owned by: Diego Alvarez (networking subteam)

- Orchestration (team: platform-engineering-orchestration)
  - Owns: desired-state store, rollout engine (canary/A-B/fallback), global policy evaluation for placement/routing, reconciliation loop to drive runtime adapters.
  - Interfaces: /v1/deploy, /v1/scale, /v1/route-eval, /v1/rollback, events stream for runtime adapters to subscribe.
  - SLOs: eventual convergence guarantees (99% within X minutes), API availability 99.9% for management-plane ops.
  - Owned by: Priya Nambiar (orchestration lead)

- Runtime Adapters (team: serving-runtime + platform-eng infra owners)
  - Adapter types: hosted-inference-adapter, dedicated-gpu-adapter, private-vpc-adapter.
  - Owns: execution lifecycle, intimate resource telemetry, fine-grained quota enforcement, KV cache semantics, adapter-side fallback to compatible model variants.
  - Required contract: adapters must implement the runtime contract (versioned) and publish capacity/cost metrics.
  - Owned by: Ethan Park (serving-runtime) + service-specific owners for private adapters.

- Policy Store (team: platform-engineering-config)
  - Owns: storage and versioning of routing/placement policies, audit logs, UI for policy edits (console). Exposes read-optimized endpoints and a write API with validation hooks.
  - Owned by: Maya Chen

- Regional Control Agents (team: platform-engineering-sre)
  - Owns: local caching, heartbeat to orchestration, emergency regional failover triggers, local health routing.
  - Should not make global placement decisions beyond cached policy; report divergences upstream.
  - Owned by: SRE lead (TBD)

Routing policy model (recommended):
- Policies are declarative JSON with fields: selector (tenant+route+model), priority, constraints (latencyBudget, costTier, regionAffinity, dataResidency), fallbackSequence (list of adapter types/model-variants), and weightings for split traffic.
- Orchestration evaluates policies to produce an ordered candidate list per request. Runtime adapters advertise capability vectors (gpuType, quantization, costPerToken, maxConcurrency) so orchestration can score match.
- Runtime decision flow (simplified): API Gateway -> Orchestration (quick-eval cache) -> selected Runtime Adapter endpoint -> adapter executes and streams back via edge.

Multi-region considerations:
- Policy semantics for regionAffinity and dataResidency must be first-class. Example: policy {dataResidency: eu, regionAffinity: [eu-west-1, eu-central-1]}.
- Cross-region failover: orchestration keeps warm adapters in secondary regions for fast failover; cost vs latency tradeoff measured per-tenant.
- Control plane HA: orchestration is global but sharded by tenant-range for performance; each shard has an active-passive pair across regions.
- Local state: runtime adapters keep ephemeral state and KV caches; orchestration keeps durable desired-state in global store with per-region read replicas.

Security + compliance boundaries:
- Private adapters must enforce tenant VPC isolation; orchestration only stores references (not customer keys). KMS integrations live with the customer-owned private agent in on-prem deployments.
- Policy writes require RBAC checks and audit trail (policy store responsibility). Console edit actions surface to audit logs and trigger a policy-validation CI job.

Observability & debugging surface:
- Trace path must include gateway_id, orchestration_eval_id, adapter_session_id. These IDs must be attached to logs and metrics across boundaries.
- Dashboards per-owner: gateway metrics, orchestration rollouts, adapter health/queue depth.
- Alerting ownership: each team owns their primary alerts; cross-cutting alerts (e.g., routing mismatch) are routed to platform-oncall with runbooks.

Failure modes and mitigations (practical notes):
- Policy store outage: serve last-known-good policies from regional agents; restrict write ops. TODO: define TTL and staleness thresholds.
- Adapter misreporting capacity: orchestration should throttle by conservative observed utilization and evict if heartbeats degrade.
- Split brain in orchestration shards: rely on leader-election (etcd/consensus) and prefer read-only operations during elections.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Exact schema for policy JSON (how expressive for cost vs latency tradeoffs?). Action: Priya to draft v1 schema (JIRA-PLAT-841).
- RBAC model for policy edits and who can create tenant-scoped fallbacks (console vs API-only).
- Autoscaling primitives exposed to adapters vs orchestration (who triggers scale-up?). Recommendation: orchestration triggers, adapters expose scale-friendly hooks.

Action items (short-term):
- Draft policy JSON schema and a reference evaluator library (go/python) — Priya (due 2026-03-18).
- Add runtime contract doc for adapters (fields, health signals, cost reporting) — Ethan (due 2026-03-22).
- Run a failure-mode tabletop for policy-store outage next sprint — SRE (Diego) to schedule.

Notes-to-self: keep the orchestration->adapter protocol minimal (10s of fields) so we can iterate adapter implementations fast. Favor push-based change notifications from orchestration to adapters for rollout speed; maintain a read cache for quick route decisions at the gateway.

References & sketches:
- See linked artifacts for drafts and PRs.
- Sketch: global orchestration shards -> regional agent caches -> adapters (hosted/dedicated/private) (hand-drawn diagram in Confluence page CONFLUENCE-PLT-142).

Unresolved: ownership of cost-metrics aggregation across adapters (central service vs adapter-side aggregation). Proposed interim: adapters publish raw counters; a central aggregator (metrics pipeline) computes per-tenant cost derivations and writes to billing system.

End of doc.
